nameStory: Swamp azalea gets its name from its love of wet, swampy places where most other flowering shrubs won't grow. The word 'azalea' comes from the Greek word 'azaleos,' meaning dry, which is ironic since this particular azalea thrives in anything but dry conditions! It's also called 'clammy azalea' because its flowers feel sticky to the touch.
description: Swamp azalea is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that grows up to 8 feet tall and equally wide, creating a rounded, bushy shape. In early summer, it produces clusters of white funnel-shaped flowers that often have a pink blush and fill the air with an incredibly sweet fragrance. The leaves are simple, oval-shaped, and have a matte green color that distinguishes them from the glossy leaves of many other shrubs. This native New England beauty is perfectly adapted to wet, acidic soils where many other plants struggle to survive.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White funnel-shaped flowers with pink blush, intensely fragrant and sticky to touch, with long prominent stamens extending beyond the petals like tiny antennae

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, matte green leaves (not glossy) that feel smooth but substantial, arranged alternately along the branches

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Rounded, multi-stemmed shrub reaching 6-8 feet tall and wide, with branches that spread outward rather than growing strictly upright

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish-brown bark on younger stems, becoming slightly rough and scaly on older main branches

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small brown capsules that split open in fall to release tiny seeds, often persisting into winter

habitat: Swamp azalea thrives in wet, acidic soils along stream banks, pond edges, wetlands, and boggy areas throughout New England. It's commonly found growing with other moisture-loving plants like red maple, elderberry, and various sedges. Unlike many azaleas that prefer well-drained soil, this species actually needs consistently moist to wet conditions and can tolerate periodic flooding.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and soft, with flower buds becoming more prominent as they prepare for their summer show.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early to mid-summer (June-July) when the intensely fragrant white flowers create spectacular displays and attract numerous pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow to reddish before dropping, and small brown seed capsules become visible and begin splitting open.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the shrub's rounded growth pattern, with small brown capsules often persisting and dark buds visible for next year's growth.

funFact: Swamp azalea flowers are so intensely fragrant that you can often smell them from 50 feet away on a calm evening - their perfume is strongest after sunset to attract night-flying moths as pollinators!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other white-flowered azaleas, but swamp azalea is the only one that thrives in consistently wet conditions. Remember: if it's blooming white and fragrant in a swamp or wet area, it's probably swamp azalea - other azaleas prefer drier ground.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'swamp honeysuckle' by some, this plant is not related to true honeysuckles at all - it's a member of the heath family along with blueberries and mountain laurel. The sticky flowers that give it the name 'clammy azalea' help ensure pollen sticks to visiting insects.
compareHints: Among New England's native azaleas, swamp azalea is unique for its white flowers and wet habitat preferences - pinxter flower and early azalea both have pink flowers and prefer drier sites. Great rhododendron has similar white flowers but much larger, evergreen leaves and grows much taller. The intense fragrance and sticky flower texture are distinctive features that set swamp azalea apart from its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its showy rhododendron and azalea cousins with their large, colorful flowers, bog Labrador tea has small white blooms and much narrower leaves.
Unlike other rhododendrons and azaleas in New England, rhodora has distinctly irregular flowers with 3 upper lobes and 2 lower petals, rather than the typical 5-petaled funnel shape.
Great rhododendron dwarfs other native rhododendrons and azaleas in New England with its massive size and evergreen leaves - most others are deciduous shrubs under 8 feet tall.

Unlike its tall cousins like Great Rhododendron or the various azaleas found in New England's lowlands, Lapland Azalea is dramatically smaller and adapted for arctic conditions rather than woodland understories.
Early azalea differs from other native azaleas by its serrated leaf edges and early bloom time.
Among New England's native azaleas, pinxter flower is distinguished by its pink color and early bloom time before leaf emergence.
Unlike the evergreen great rhododendron with its large leathery leaves and white flowers, flame azalea loses its leaves in winter and produces much more intensely colored blooms.

Among New England's rhododendrons and azaleas, pinkshell azalea stands out for its soft pink, shell-like flowers and graceful, open growth habit - most other azaleas are either denser in form or have different flower colors and textures.
Among New England's rhododendrons and azaleas, Catawba rhododendron is distinguished by its purple flowers and evergreen leaves.
Among New England rhododendrons, Carolina rhododendron stands out for its small, compact size and late spring bloom time.
Unlike our native azaleas which tend to have pink, white, or orange flowers, red azalea stands out with its intense red blooms.
